strengths: The paper presents a simple, well-motivated data-centric idea: quantifying per-sample and per-token visual dependency via the loss difference between conditioning with the true image vs. a blurred image, and using it to filter samples and mask tokens during instruction tuning. The metric is model-agnostic, decomposable, and easy to compute.

The empirical evaluation is thorough and well-controlled: three LVLMs (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B), seven benchmarks spanning vision understanding and hallucination, a random-subset ablation that isolates the effect of VIG-based selection (Table 5/E.1), a selection-ratio sweep (E.2), composability with inference-time methods (VCD, PAI, VAR) and a training-based method (LACING), and mechanistic analyses (attention to visual tokens, robustness to textual corruption).

Validation of the metric itself is convincing: Table 1 shows VIG varies sensibly with image-answer alignment, Figure 2 shows VIG distributions align with known benchmark modality dependencies, and Table 2/Figure 3 show token-level gains concentrate on visually salient tokens (colors, spatial relations) versus syntactic tokens.

Reproducibility is strong: selection thresholds are reported (Tables C.1, E.2), training hyperparameters match original implementations, compute costs are quantified (6 GPU-hours for scoring), and pretrained checkpoints are identified. The limitations discussion (compute overhead, restriction to LLaVA/ShareGPT4V families) is honest and specific.
weaknesses: Novelty concerns relative to prior work: VIG is essentially pointwise V-usable information (Xu et al., 2020; Ethayarajh & Jurafsky, 2022), i.e., the difference in expected loss with and without conditioning on the input, applied at sample and token levels. This line of work is not cited or discussed, so the conceptual contribution is overstated as new; the contribution is best viewed as an adaptation/application of an existing information-theoretic quantity to LVLM training data curation.

The text-only conditioning is simulated with a Gaussian-blurred image (following Xing et al.), but the paper provides no sensitivity analysis of this choice. A blurred image still contains color, layout, and low-frequency statistics, so PPL(A|Q) is not purely linguistic; how strongly the VIG ranking (and thus all downstream results) depends on the blur strength is unexamined.

Gains are modest on several benchmarks and statistical significance is not addressed: e.g., DocVQA +0.20 and POPE F1 +0.03 for LLaVA-1.5 7B (Table 3), and GPT-4-based scores (LLaVAW, MMVet, MMHal) carry evaluation variance that is not quantified. Multiple seeds or variance estimates are absent.

The 'theoretical foundation' (Eqs. 4-5) is a straightforward cross-entropy/KL decomposition under a deterministic (Dirac) target distribution; it adds limited insight and is somewhat overclaimed as theory.

Potential harms of aggressive token masking are not evaluated: no language-only or instruction-following benchmark is included, so it is unclear whether removing low-VIG tokens from the loss degrades linguistic competence, and only a single ratio (p=70) is used for the main results without justification beyond the ablation on 4 benchmarks.

VIG is computed with the model after pretraining, which introduces a mild circularity: if the pretrained adapter already has biases, the selected data reflects that model's notion of visual dependency; the transferability of the selection across alignment stages is not analyzed.

Missing comparison with other data-selection/pruning baselines for multimodal instruction tuning (beyond a random subset), which would better position the practical benefit of VIG-based selection relative to alternative curation signals.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: VIG provides a simple, model-agnostic, decomposable quantity (log-ratio of perplexities with vs. without visual input) that can be computed per sample and per token, and the paper shows it behaves sensibly (Table 1, Figure 2, Table 2).

The evaluation covers multiple models (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B), both vision-understanding and hallucination benchmarks, and includes useful ablations (sample vs. token-level selection, selection ratio p, Random/SS/SS+TS).

Comparison against both training-free (VCD, PAI, VAR) and training-based (LACING) grounding methods, plus a demonstration of orthogonality when combined with them (Table 4), strengthens the empirical case.

Mechanistic corroboration (visual-token attention fraction, corruption-robustness test) and qualitative examples support the claim that the method improves grounding rather than just shifting benchmarks.

Implementation details (thresholds, hyperparameters, compute overhead of VIG scoring) are reported, and the limitations section honestly acknowledges scope restrictions (LLaVA/ShareGPT4V families, computational overhead).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: token-level VIG is essentially a pointwise mutual information quantity between the image and answer tokens computed under the current model, and the training scheme is a direct multimodal adaptation of selective/loss-based token filtering (e.g., RHO-loss and 'Not all tokens are what you need', cited as [52]). The 'theoretical foundation' in Eqs. 4-5 is a trivial entropy/KL decomposition and does not add substantive insight.

The operationalization of 'absence of visual information' via a Gaussian-blurred image is questionable: blur may retain low-level cues, induces distribution shift for the vision encoder, and could distort both sample- and token-level VIG. No sensitivity analysis to blur parameters is provided, and a true text-only conditioning baseline is not compared.

Missing critical baselines for the selection strategy: no comparison against selecting samples/tokens by text-only perplexity, loss magnitude, answer length, or general data-quality filters. Without these, it is unclear whether VIG specifically (rather than 'any informativeness filter') drives the gains.

Gains are modest and sometimes marginal (DocVQA +0.20, POPE F1 +0.03 for LLaVA-1.5 7B), yet no variance, seeds, or statistical significance is reported; single-run results on small GPT-judged benchmarks (LLaVAW has 60 questions, MMHal 96) could easily fall within noise.

Internal inconsistencies and overclaims: Table 5 and Table E.1 report different numbers for the same Random and SS settings (e.g., LLaVAW 56.91 vs. 58.50 for Random), and the text claims all reduced-ratio models outperform the baseline on hallucination benchmarks even though POPE F1 at p=30 (82.80) is well below the baseline (85.90).

A potential circularity concern is unaddressed: VIG is computed with the aligned (pretrained) model, so high-VIG data selection optimizes for what the current model finds visually useful, which may bias toward easy or redundant visual patterns rather than genuinely valuable, diverse supervision; generalization to other architectures is untested (acknowledged as a limitation but not explored even on one additional family).
Some evaluation details are underspecified for reproducibility (e.g., captioning prompt and protocol for CHAIR, exact MMHal grading pipeline), and no code or data-release statement is provided.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated data-centric contribution: VIG provides a simple, model-agnostic, decomposable metric (perplexity/loss reduction from visual conditioning) that quantifies visual dependency at both sample and token levels, filling a genuine gap relative to prior decoding- and architecture-based bias mitigation work.

Thorough empirical validation of the metric itself: VIG is shown to be sensitive to the degree of visual grounding (Table 1), consistent with known benchmark-level modality dependencies (Figure 2), and token-level decompositions recover intuitively visually grounded tokens (colors, spatial relations, attributes) vs. syntactic tokens (Table 2, Figure 3).

Strong and carefully controlled experiments: results span three models (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B) and seven benchmarks, with an essential ablation (Random 70% vs. SS vs. SS+TS in Tables 5/E.1) that isolates the benefit of VIG-based selection from mere data reduction, and a selection-ratio sweep (Table E.3) showing robustness across p.

Demonstrated orthogonality: VIG training combines additively with training-free methods (VCD, PAI, VAR) and the training-based LACING (Table 4), supporting the claim that it is a data-level enhancement complementary to existing approaches.

Mechanistic corroboration: increased attention fraction on visual tokens (Figure 4, D.1) and improved robustness under textual corruption (Figure 5, D.2) provide converging evidence that the method strengthens visual grounding rather than merely exploiting benchmark idiosyncrasies.

Honest limitations discussion (VIG computation overhead, restricted model families) and reasonably detailed implementation settings (thresholds, hyperparameters, hardware) in the appendix support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Magnitude of gains is uneven and sometimes within plausible noise: e.g., POPE F1 for LLaVA-1.5 7B improves by only +0.03 and DocVQA by +0.20, yet the paper claims improvements 'on all benchmarks'; no variance or multiple-seed reporting is provided for any comparison, making small deltas hard to interpret.

The visual-absence surrogate (Gaussian blur) is the crux of the metric but is not critically validated: blur removes fine detail while potentially preserving coarse shape/color/layout, so 'VIG' may partially measure sensitivity to image statistics rather than semantic visual dependency; no comparison against alternatives (e.g., noise, shuffled images, text-only LLM) is given.

A potential confound is underexplored: token-level selection discards low-VIG tokens, which tend to be frequent syntactic/function tokens; this changes the effective data distribution (e.g., toward caption-like data, which aligns with COCO/CHAIR/LLaVAW gains) and could explain MMBench degradation at aggressive ratios (p=30, 50) rather than pure 'data quality' effects.

The 'larger models use selected data more effectively' interpretation for LLaVA-1.5 13B (12.14M active tokens) is speculative and not directly tested; per-model optimal p is not investigated for 13B/ShareGPT4V.
Generalization beyond the LLaVA/ShareGPT4V family (both Qwen/Vicuna-based, CLIP encoders) is untested; the authors acknowledge this, but it limits the claimed model-agnostic scope of VIG.

No statement about code/checkpoint release; given that VIG scoring details (blur parameters 'scaled to input resolution') are only partially specified, exact reproducibility would benefit from released artifacts.
Benchmark suite relies on GPT-based judges (LLaVAW, MMVet, MMHal) with older/possibly inconsistent judge versions; judged evaluation introduces additional uncertainty for the small reported gains.

strengths: The core idea is clean and useful: VIG (log-ratio of perplexities with vs. without visual conditioning) is an interpretable, model-agnostic, and token-decomposable measure of visual dependency, and the paper derives its connection to cross-entropy/KL divergence in a transparent way.

The empirical validation is unusually thorough: four different LVLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B, Open-Qwen2VL 2B), a mix of vision-understanding and hallucination benchmarks, and careful ablations (Random vs. sample-level vs. sample+token selection; selection ratio p; combination with VCD/PAI/VAR/LACING).

The analysis section goes beyond headline numbers: benchmark-level VIG distributions (Fig. 2), token-level decomposition with POS analysis (Figs. 3–4), attention-to-visual-token fractions, the 'blind faith in text' corruption protocol, and a data-distribution analysis showing that filtering preserves long-tail concepts while reshaping task composition (OCR-VQA/TextVQA retained, GQA filtered).

The ablation clearly isolates the contribution of each component: Random-70% degrades performance while VIG-based SS+TS improves it, and the additive gains when combined with inference-time methods support the claim of orthogonality.

Limitations are discussed honestly (compute overhead of VIG scoring, focus on LLaVA/ShareGPT4V families), and implementation details (thresholds τ_p per model, hyperparameters, compute costs, checkpoints) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Originality is moderate. The selective-training mechanism is essentially sample filtering plus per-token loss masking, closely following Selective Language Modeling (Lin et al., 2024); the novelty lies mainly in transferring the loss-difference idea to visual grounding via a blurred-image contrast, which is itself borrowed from Xing et al. (2025). The theoretical derivation (Eqs. 3–6) is largely straightforward algebra on the definition.

The 'absence of visual information' is simulated by a blurred image rather than removing the visual tokens. The paper does not justify why blur is preferable to zeroing/blanking the visual embedding, nor does it report how sensitive VIG scores are to this design choice; the resulting rankings of samples/tokens could differ under other ablations of the visual input.

Some reported gains are small relative to plausible evaluation noise (e.g., POPE F1 +0.03, DocVQA +0.20 for LLaVA-1.5 7B; MMBench +0.87), yet the paper claims 'improves performance on all benchmarks' and 'superior performance across all benchmarks'. There are no error bars, seed repetitions, or significance tests, so several claims of strict improvement are not statistically supported.

The very strong efficiency claim (LLaVA-1.5 13B trained on only 21% of tokens, +79% reduction in active tokens, yet improving on every benchmark) is striking and deserves deeper investigation; the paper offers limited analysis of why token selection yields such large gains, and it is not clear how much of the effect comes from denoising LLM-generated noisy supervision vs. visual grounding per se.

Reusing the same threshold τ_p for both sample-level selection and token-level masking is justified only as avoiding an extra hyperparameter; given that token-level selection dominates the gains (Tab. 6: SS MMBench 57.56 vs. SS+TS 66.33), a dedicated token-threshold ablation would strengthen the design justification.

VIG is computed with a fixed pretrained (pre-instruction-tuning) model, and the threshold τ_70 takes near-zero or negative values for several models (e.g., −0.042 for ShareGPT4V), meaning samples where the image actively hurts loss are also retained; the semantics of selection near a negative threshold are not fully discussed.
Text-only results (Tab. E.2) repeat identical GSM8K/MMLU/HellaSwag numbers for LLaVA-1.5 7B and 13B rows, which appears to be a copy error and slightly undermines confidence in the reporting.

strengths: Well-motivated data-centric framing: quantifying visual dependency of training samples/tokens is a sensible and useful angle for the language-bias problem, and VIG is simple, model-agnostic, and cheap to compute.

Comprehensive empirical program: results across four models (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B, Open-Qwen2VL 2B), a broad benchmark suite (vision understanding + hallucination), comparison with training-free and training-based baselines, and several sanity checks (text-only benchmark preservation, long-tail concept retention, task-level retention analysis, attention analysis, 'blind faith in text' robustness).
The token-level decomposition (Eq. 6) and POS analysis (Fig. 4, Tab. 2) provide a plausible and interpretable validation that VIG tracks visually grounded tokens rather than artifacts.
Honest limitations discussion: computational overhead of VIG scoring, scope restricted to LLaVA-1.5/ShareGPT4V families, and an explicit impact statement.
Generally clear writing with detailed reproducibility information in appendices (thresholds, hyperparameters, hardware, checkpoints).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core signal (loss/perplexity difference with vs. without visual input) is well established in the literature (e.g., Xing et al. 2025, which they adopt for the blurred-image condition; contrastive-decoding line; Madaan et al. 2025), and the selective token training is a direct multimodal adaptation of Lin et al. (2024)'s selective language modeling, which they cite. The paper's contribution is mostly an empirical bundling of known components.

The theoretical derivation (Sec. 3.2, Eqs. 4-5) is largely cosmetic: under their own Dirac-delta assumption the entropy terms vanish and everything reduces to the trivial statement that VIG equals the loss difference. It adds little insight or falsifiable content.

Key claims are weaker than the evidence. 'Superior performance with highly sparse supervision' rests mainly on LLaVA's known insensitivity to instruction-data reduction: the Random-70% ablation only mildly degrades the baseline, and the SS-only setting barely beats Random (e.g., MMBench 57.56 vs 55.97; Table 6 vs. F.1), suggesting most of the gain comes from token masking, not VIG-based sample selection.

Several per-benchmark gains are marginal or within plausible noise (e.g., POPE Acc. +0.03 and DocVQA +0.20 for LLaVA-1.5 7B; CI +0.03 for 13B), and there are no seeds/variance/significance analyses anywhere in the paper.
Inconsistency in reported numbers: Table 6 lists Random/SS LLaVAW as 56.91/58.12 while the same ablation in Table F.1 reports 58.50/58.71, undermining confidence in the reporting pipeline.

Potential circularity and confounds are not analyzed: VIG scores are computed with the same aligned model used for training; the blurred-image 'visual absence' condition still feeds a (degraded) visual embedding through the adapter, which may confound 'visual information' with distributional shift of the visual prefix. No validation of the blur against a true no-image condition is reported.
GPT-based evaluation (GPT-4o/0613 for LLaVAW/MMVet/MMHal) with small test sets (24 images/60 questions for LLaVAW, 96 for MMHal) makes some of the headline improvements fragile.

Scale and generalization: no experiments on modern, stronger architectures (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, Cambrian, etc.) or open-ended reasoning settings; the 'architecture-agnostic' claim is supported only by one small 2B model on a single extra dataset.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated central idea: VIG provides a simple, model-agnostic, decomposable measure of how much each sample/token benefits from visual input, directly addressing an underexplored gap between data-centric filtering and visual grounding.

The analysis section (Sec. 3.3) convincingly validates the metric: benchmark-level VIG distributions align with known modality dependencies (Fig. 2), token-level gains concentrate on visually grounded content (colors, spatial relations, states) per Tables 2, 4, and Fig. 3-4.

Strong empirical coverage: results across four architectures (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, ShareGPT4V 7B, Open-Qwen2VL 2B) and datasets show consistent improvements while using far fewer tokens (e.g., 12.14M active tokens for 13B, -79%), with a Random-subset ablation (Tab. 6/F.1) and selection-ratio sweep (Fig. 7, Tab. F.3) that isolate the effect of VIG selection from mere data reduction.

Good mechanistic follow-through: increased attention to visual tokens (Fig. 5, E.1), robustness to textual corruption (Fig. 6, E.2, Tab. E.1 vs. VCD), preserved text-only performance (Tab. 5/E.2), and distribution analysis showing long-tail concepts are preserved (E.4) collectively support the claimed mechanism rather than just aggregate scores.

Demonstrated orthogonality/complementarity with training-free (VCD, PAI, VAR) and training-based (LACING) baselines (Tab. 4), and an honest limitations section (VIG computation overhead, empirical scope limited to LLaVA/ShareGPT4V families).
weaknesses: The theoretical framing (Eqs. 4-5) is largely cosmetic: under a one-hot target the entropy terms vanish and the 'KL-based' derivation collapses to the trivial identity that VIG equals the loss difference. It does not provide non-trivial insight beyond Eq. 3/6, so the paper's 'theoretical foundation' claim overstates the contribution.

VIG relies on Gaussian blurring as a proxy for visual absence; this removes high-frequency cues but may retain low-level statistics or bias-based information, and the sensitivity of conclusions to the blur choice is not ablated. Using the empirical loss gap of a fixed pretrained (aligned-stage) model as ground truth for 'visual dependency' is a heuristic whose own biases are unexamined.

Some gains are marginal and presented without statistical significance or variance across seeds (e.g., POPE Acc. +0.03/+0.39, DocVQA +0.20 on 7B in Tab. 3); a few cells are small enough to be within noise, which weakens the 'improves on all benchmarks' claim.

A potential confounder is under-discussed: the task-level distribution shift (OCR-VQA 98.4%, TextVQA 92.6% retained vs. GQA 44.2% in E.4) could itself explain the DocVQA/vision gains, i.e., the improvement may partly reflect favoring dense-visual task types rather than a general grounding mechanism; no re-weighting control is provided.
Minor numerical inconsistency: Random-subset LLaVAW is 56.91 in Tab. 6 but 58.50 in Appendix Tab. F.1; such discrepancies undermine confidence in reported numbers.

The method is essentially an application of selective language modeling (Rho-1, Lin et al. 2024) to LVLMs with a visual-gain criterion; the core algorithmic novelty is incremental, with the contribution resting mainly on the metric definition and empirical validation.

The single shared threshold tau_p at both sample and token levels is convenient but means the token-level 'selection' threshold can be negative (Tab. D.1), so tokens with negative visual gain are still trained on in some models; a proper sensitivity analysis of decoupling these thresholds is missing.
